semantic_correction.stem: A nurse explains routine newborn hearing screening to new parents. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: Hearing screening is reserved for newborns with a family history or another recognized risk factor for hearing loss.
options.B: Newborns should complete hearing screening by 1 month of age, with timely diagnostic follow-up if they do not pass.
options.C: Hearing screening should be deferred until speech delay becomes apparent because newborn testing is not reliable enough.
options.D: Routine newborn screening has little value because congenital hearing loss cannot be identified during the newborn period.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC Early Hearing Detection and Intervention guidance uses the 1-3-6 benchmarks: hearing screening by 1 month of age, diagnostic hearing evaluation by 3 months for infants who do not pass screening, and early intervention by 6 months for infants with confirmed hearing loss. CDC materials emphasize early identification for all infants rather than waiting for speech delay or limiting screening to those with known risk factors. Therefore option B is accurate.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain the universal newborn hearing-screening benchmark and the importance of timely diagnostic follow-up when a newborn does not pass screening.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Early Hearing Detection and Intervention 1-3-6 Benchmarks; Hearing Loss in Infants and Young Children: Considerations for Pediatric Primary Care Providers
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current CDC EHDI resources accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: EHDI 1-3-6 benchmarks — hearing screening by 1 month, hearing evaluation by 3 months for infants who do not pass, and early intervention by 6 months when hearing loss is confirmed. Pediatric primary care considerations — obtain hearing screen no later than 1 month if not already completed; refer for diagnostic audiologic evaluation no later than 3 months after failed screening
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC supports hearing screening for all infants by 1 month of age, diagnostic evaluation by 3 months when screening is not passed, and early intervention by 6 months when hearing loss is confirmed.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: shortened the uniquely long correct answer, removed the family-history-only misconception, and preserved the CDC 1-3-6 screening/follow-up benchmarks.

audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — newborn screening
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests universal newborn hearing screening and timely follow-up without a correct-answer length cue.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. Newborn hearing screening is not limited to infants with known risk factors or family history.
option_audit.B: Correct. It matches the CDC 1-month screening and timely diagnostic follow-up benchmark.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Screening is intended to identify hearing loss before speech delay becomes apparent.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Congenital hearing loss can be detected through newborn screening and diagnostic evaluation.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. B alone matches the CDC EHDI timing and universal-screening intent.
cueing_check: All four options are newborn-hearing-screening statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies B.
